analysis.one_liner: Caps Western wholesale electricity prices and refunds overcharges to California consumers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received any committee action and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2000 electricity price spike in San Diego, this bill would have required federal regulators to set a maximum wholesale electricity price for the Western market, roughly returning it to pre-crisis levels. Sellers who charged more would have had to refund the excess, with the money passed down to the consumers who paid the inflated bills. Sellers who violated the law would have faced penalties worth three times the amount involved.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary electricity customers in San Diego and the rest of the Western grid, who were paying sharply inflated rates after retail price controls were lifted in 2000, would have gotten direct refunds of overcharges and lower wholesale prices passed through to their bills.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to establish a maximum wholesale electricity price for the Western System Coordinating Council, set at the lesser of the pre-crisis three-year average price or a cost-based rate under the Federal Power Act.

Requires any seller that charged above the maximum to promptly refund the full overcharge, with the money passed through to ultimate consumers, and imposes civil penalties equal to three times the value of any violation.

analysis.who_pays: Wholesale electricity sellers—power generators and energy marketers selling into the Western market—would have paid refunds of past overcharges, sold under a price cap going forward, and faced treble penalties for violations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wholesale power generators and energy marketers

drawbacks.text: A hard price cap set below crisis-level market prices can discourage generators from selling into a shortage area or investing in new supply, which some economists warned could deepen the very shortages driving the 2000 price spike in California.

The bill set a deadline of November 30, 2000 for the price order and required the maximum to equal the lower of a historical average or a cost-based formula, leaving regulators little room to account for genuinely higher fuel costs at the time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers facing doubled and tripled electric bills in San Diego, the refund and cap provisions offered immediate, direct relief, and the treble penalty gave the cap real teeth. The main honest concern is that a rigid price cap during a genuine supply shortage can scare supply away or delay new investment, so the cap needed to be set carefully. On balance the bill would have shifted substantial costs away from households and onto sellers who had collected crisis-level prices, though as a hastily drafted, single-session bill its details would likely have required refinement.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee in September 2000, but the committee never took it up, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Barbara Boxer introduced the HELP San Diego Act on September 21, 2000, during the electricity price spike in San Diego.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day.
The committee took no further action on the bill, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 without the bill ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wholesale electricity sellers kept the above-market prices they had charged during the 2000 spike, with no refunds or caps, while San Diego households continued paying inflated rates until regulators acted on their own later.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wholesale power sellers, not San Diego consumers

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.role: U.S. Senator from California; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap Western wholesale electricity prices and refund overcharges to consumers, and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 21, 2000 and never reported it out, held no vote, and let it die at the end of the 106th Congress.

against.name: Sen. Frank Murkowski
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill during the roughly three and a half months remaining in the Congress.

against.name: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission leadership
against.role: Federal regulator the bill would have compelled to set price caps
against.what_they_did: Resisted mandating wholesale price caps during the 2000-2001 California energy crisis, arguing against broad caps even as the crisis continued.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote; its support was limited to its Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, so no partisan split can be measured from the record.

industries.industry: Wholesale electricity sellers (merchant generators and energy marketers)
industries.note: The bill would have rolled their selling prices back to roughly pre-crisis levels, forced refunds of every dollar collected above the cap since June 1, 2000, and exposed them to penalties worth three times the violation amount. Those sellers had been collecting sharply inflated prices from California buyers during the 2000 spike.

industries.industry: Retail electric utilities and municipal purchasers
industries.note: Utilities that bought at wholesale and resold to customers would have had to pass refunds through rather than keep them, but they would also have paid less for power going forward under the cap. California's retail customers, who bore the crisis-level rates, come out ahead either way.
